claim: There are differences in pruriceptive processing between primates and rodents.

claim: The results do not support the spatial contrast theory of coding of itch and pain.
source: Our results provide evidence for differences in pruriceptive processing between primates and rodents, and do not support the spatial contrast theory of coding of itch and pain.
evidence: This conclusion is based on psychophysical experiments showing that combinations of pruritogens did not alter sensations as predicted by the spatial contrast theory.

claim: The sensations of itch and pain serve a similar purpose, which is to alert the organism of potentially harmful external threats.
source: The sensations of itch and pain serve a similar purpose, which is to alert the organism of potentially harmful external threats.

claim: In humans and other primates, multiple types of nociceptive primary afferents including unmyelinated and myelinated nerve fibers appear to have a role in itch sensation.
source: In humans and other primates, multiple types of nociceptive primary afferents including unmyelinated and myelinated nerve fibers appear to have a role in itch sensation (Johanek et al., 2008; Johanek et al., 2007; Namer et al., 2008; Ringkamp et al., 2011; Schmelz et al., 1997; Wooten et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Histamine and nonhistaminergic pruritogens activate distinct sets of nociceptive primary afferents.
source: Moreover, HIS and nonhistaminergic pruritogens activate distinct sets of nociceptive primary afferents, including mechano-insensitive C fibers (C-MIAs), CMHs, mechanosensitive A-fiber nociceptors (A-MSAs), and spinothalamic projection neurons (Davidson et al., 2007; Johanek et al., 2008; Namer et al., 2008; Schmelz et al., 1997; Wooten et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: The spatial contrast model posits that neuronal activity from a spatially restricted set of nociceptive afferents is interpreted as 'itch,' whereas activity from a spatially larger pool of afferents is interpreted as 'pain'.
source: Among the models that have been proposed to explain this conundrum (for review, see Carstens et al., 2020; LaMotte et al., 2014), the spatial contrast model posits that neuronal activity from a spatially restricted set of nociceptive afferents is interpreted as 'itch,' whereas activity from a spatially larger pool of afferents is interpreted as 'pain' (Namer et al., 2008; Namer and Reeh, 2013; Steinhoff et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a description of the spatial contrast model supported by citations.

claim: Human DRG neurons co-express both MRGPRD and MRGPRX1.

claim: Human DRG neurons co-express MRGPRD, MRGPRX1, and TRPV1.

source: Further, injection of ALA and BAM8-22 into the receptive fields (RFs) of nociceptors in nonhuman primate revealed that QCs respond to ALA, and SCs preferentially respond to BAM8-22, with a large degree of overlap.

claim: There is a large degree of overlap in the responses of QCs and SCs to ALA and BAM8-22 in nonhuman primates.
source: Further, injection of ALA and BAM8-22 into the receptive fields (RFs) of nociceptors in nonhuman primate revealed that QCs respond to ALA, and SCs preferentially respond to BAM8-22, with a large degree of overlap.
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological recordings presented in the study.

claim: In primates, histamine and cowhage activate largely non-overlapping spinothalamic tract (STT) neurons.
source: In addition, in primates, HIS and cowhage activate largely non-overlapping spinothalamic tract (STT) neurons (Davidson et al., 2012).

claim: Humans and nonhuman primates do not have either the rodent Mrgpra or Mrgprc subfamilies of receptors.
source: The representation of the MRGPR families of receptors in humans and nonhuman primates differs from rodents in that they contain a distinct MRGPRX subfamily of receptors that is absent in rodents and that they do not have either the rodent Mrgpra or Mrgprc subfamilies of receptors (Figure 1A; Solinski et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 1A and a citation to Solinski et al., 2014.

claim: CMHs can be classified into two distinct subtypes, QCs and SCs, based on responses to a stepped heat stimulus.
source: Based on responses to a stepped heat stimulus (49°C, 3 s, Figure 3A), CMHs can be classified into two distinct subtypes, QCs and SCs (Wooten et al., 2014).
evidence: This is based on a classification method described in Wooten et al., 2014 and applied in this study.

claim: Heat responses of QCs exhibit a burst of discharge at the onset of the heat stimulus with the discharge adapting during the stimulus plateau.
source: Briefly, heat responses of QCs exhibit a burst of discharge at the onset of the heat stimulus with the discharge adapting during the stimulus plateau.
evidence: This is a description of the characteristic response of QCs to heat stimuli.

claim: SCs typically have a slower response onset, do not exhibit a burst at the onset of the stimulus, and the peak discharge occurs during the plateau phase of the stimulus.
source: SCs typically have a slower response onset, do not exhibit a burst at the onset of the stimulus, and the peak discharge occurs during the plateau phase of the stimulus (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a description of the characteristic response of SCs to heat stimuli shown in Figure 3B.

claim: For 31/66 CMHs, the time of peak discharge fell above the line of equality, and these afferents were classified as 'SC'.
source: For 31/66 CMHs, the time of peak discharge fell above the line of equality (Figure 3C, black line), indicating that the peak discharge occurred during the plateau phase of the stimulus, and these afferents were therefore classified as 'SC' (Figure 3C, blue circles).
evidence: This is based on classification of CMHs using heat response data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: 29 out of 66 CMH fibers exhibited a burst of discharge at the onset and then an adapting response, and these afferents were classified as 'QC'.
source: 29 out of 66 CMH fibers exhibited a burst of discharge at the onset and then an adapting response, and these afferents were classified as 'QC' (Figure 3C, red circles).
evidence: This is based on classification of CMHs using heat response data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: For 26/29 QCs, the time of peak discharge fell below or close to the line of equality, indicating occurrence of peak discharge during or at the end of the rising phase of the temperature ramp.
source: For 26/29 QCs, the time of peak discharge fell below or close to the line of equality, indicating occurrence of peak discharge during or at the end of the rising phase of the temperature ramp.
evidence: This is based on analysis of heat response data from QCs.

claim: Six CMHs were labeled as 'unclassified' because the time of peak discharge fell close to the line of equality and they did not exhibit an initial burst discharge typical of a QC response.

evidence: This is based on classification of CMHs using heat response data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The two subpopulations of CMHs, QCs and SCs, differed in their responses to injections of ALA and BAM8-22 into their cutaneous receptive fields.

evidence: This is based on analysis of electrophysiological data comparing ALA and BAM8-22 responses.

claim: ALA responses in only seven SCs fulfilled the criterion of a positive response (≥10 APs).

evidence: This is based on analysis of electrophysiological data from SCs.

claim: Responses to ALA and BAM8-22 differed significantly within and across fiber types (QCs and SCs).
source: Responses to ALA and BAM8-22 differed significantly within and across fiber types (Figure 4B, repeated measures ANOVA (RMANOVA) with' fiber type' as a between-subjects factor and' pruritogen' as within-subjects factor; interaction: F(1,58)=29.55, p<0.001).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of electrophysiological data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: For SCs, responses to BAM8-22 were significantly larger than those to ALA.
source: Post hoc analysis revealed that for SCs (n = 31), responses to BAM8-22 were significantly larger than those to ALA (94.00 ± 12.01 APs vs. 10.32 ± 3.22 APs, p<0.001, Scheffe test).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of electrophysiological data.

claim: In QCs, responses to ALA did not significantly differ from those to BAM8-22.
source: In QCs (n = 29), responses to ALA did not significantly differ from those to BAM8-22 (83.38 ± 8.42 APs vs. 51.97 ± 11.17 APs, respectively; p=0.25).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of electrophysiological data.

claim: Between populations, responses to ALA were significantly larger in QCs than SCs.
source: Between populations, responses to ALA were significantly larger in QCs than SCs (p<0.001, Scheffe test)
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of electrophysiological data.

claim: Between populations, responses to BAM8-22 were significantly larger in SCs than QCs.
source: whereas responses to BAM8-22 were significantly larger in SCs than QCs (p=0.021, Scheffe test).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of electrophysiological data.

claim: ALA activated 27/29 QCs.
source: ALA activated 27/29 QCs and 19 of these responded also to BAM8-22 (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 4C.

claim: 19 QCs responded to both ALA and BAM8-22.
source: ALA activated 27/29 QCs and 19 of these responded also to BAM8-22 (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Two QCs were only responsive to BAM8-22.
source: Two QCs were only responsive to BAM8-22.
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological recordings.

claim: Only 7/31 SCs responded to ALA.
source: In contrast, only 7/31 SCs responded to ALA with 6 of these being also responsive to BAM8-22
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological recordings.

claim: 6 SCs responded to both ALA and BAM8-22.
source: In contrast, only 7/31 SCs responded to ALA with 6 of these being also responsive to BAM8-22
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological recordings.

claim: 23/31 SCs responded only to BAM8-22.
source: whereas 23/31 SCs responded only to BAM8-22.
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological recordings.

claim: One of 31 SCs did not respond to either ALA or BAM8-22.
source: One of 31 SCs did not respond to either agonist.
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological recordings.

claim: At the doses tested, QCs and SCs are preferentially activated by ALA and BAM8-22, respectively.
source: Taken together, these findings suggest that, at the doses tested, QCs and SCs are preferentially activated by ALA and BAM8-22, respectively.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the electrophysiological data.

claim: QCs may represent fibers expressing both MRGPRs at the peripheral terminals, but preferentially MRGPRD.
source: The data imply that QCs may represent fibers expressing both MRGPRs at the peripheral terminals, but preferentially MRGPRD, whereas SCs may preferentially express MRGPRX1.
evidence: This is an inference based on the electrophysiological response patterns.

claim: SCs may preferentially express MRGPRX1.
source: The data imply that QCs may represent fibers expressing both MRGPRs at the peripheral terminals, but preferentially MRGPRD, whereas SCs may preferentially express MRGPRX1.
evidence: This is an inference based on the electrophysiological response patterns.

claim: About half of the CMH neurons tested responded to both BAM8-22 and ALA.
source: To summarize, in contrast to our human ISH data that suggested nearly 100% overlap of MRGPRX1 and MRGPRD expression, we found that only about half of the CMH neurons tested responded to both BAM8-22 and ALA.
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological recordings from CMHs.

claim: All mechanosensitive C-fibers responsive to BAM8-22 or ALA responded to noxious heat.
source: Furthermore, in accordance with MRGPRD and MRGPRX1 neurons expressing TRPV1, all of these mechanosensitive C-fibers responded to noxious heat regardless of the selectivity of their responses to BAM8-22 or ALA.
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological recordings showing heat responses in these fibers.

claim: Seven C-MIAs were tested with ALA and none responded.
source: We previously reported that seven C-MIAs were tested with ALA and that none responded (Wooten et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wooten et al., 2014.

claim: Of six C-MIAs tested with BAM8-22, two responded.
source: Of six C-MIAs tested with BAM8-22 in this study, all were tested with heat and four responded. Two of six C-MIAs (one responsive to heat) responded to BAM8-22.
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological recordings from C-MIAs.

claim: Of 16 A-MSAs tested, one responded to ALA.
source: Of the 16 A-MSAs, one responded to ALA (5 min net response of 14 APs)
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological recordings from A-MSAs.

claim: Of 16 A-MSAs tested, one responded to BAM8-22.
source: and another to BAM8-22 with 129 APs within the first 30 s after injection but no activity thereafter.
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological recordings from A-MSAs.

claim: Of eight A-MIAs tested, none responded to ALA or BAM8-22.
source: Of the eight A-MIAs, none responded to ALA or BAM8-22.
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological recordings from A-MIAs.

claim: A-fiber nociceptors and C-MIAs are likely minor contributors to the sensations caused by ALA and BAM8-22.
source: These data suggest that A-fiber nociceptors and C-MIAs are likely minor contributors to the sensations caused by these compounds.
evidence: This is an inference based on the low responsiveness of these fiber types to ALA and BAM8-22.

claim: The majority of subjects reported itch and nociceptive sensations after the administration of a single pruritogen and after the combinations thereof.
source: The majority of subjects reported itch and nociceptive sensations after the administration of a single pruritogen and after the combinations thereof.
evidence: This is based on psychophysical data from human subjects.

claim: The number of subjects reporting itch or nociceptive sensations did not differ between stimuli (single pruritogens vs. combinations).
source: The number of subjects reporting these sensations did not differ between stimuli (Figure 5A), and the number of subjects experiencing itch or nociceptive sensations did not change when combinations of pruritogens were applied.
evidence: This is based on psychophysical data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: For the co-administration of BAM8-22 and ALA, the temporal profiles of the different sensations were visibly similar compared to those evoked by BAM8-22 or ALA alone.
source: For the co-administration of BAM8-22 and ALA, the temporal profiles of the different sensations were visibly similar compared to those evoked by BAM8-22 or ALA alone, peaking within the first minute after application and decreasing slowly over approximately 10 min (Figure 5B–D).
evidence: This is based on psychophysical data shown in Figures 5B-D.

claim: HIS-induced itch peaked within the first minute after injection but appeared to decline much slower over 20 min.
source: Similarly, HIS-induced itch peaked within the first minute after injection but appeared to decline much slower over 20 min (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is based on psychophysical data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The temporal profile of the itch sensation produced by the triple combination was similar to that of the BAM8-22 + ALA combination, except that the decline of itch sensation appeared to be slower.
source: The temporal profile of the itch sensation produced by the triple combination was similar to that of the BAM8-22 + ALA combination, except that the decline of itch sensation appeared to be slower (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is based on psychophysical data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Peak magnitude of perceived sensation intensity was not significantly different for the five different stimuli (three single pruritogens and two combinations).
source: Peak magnitude of perceived sensation intensity (n = 29), (I) computed area under the curve (n = 17), or (J) duration of itch, stinging/pricking, or burn ratings (n = 17) were each not significantly different for the five different stimuli, that is, three single pruritogens and two combinations (repeated measures ANOVA [RMANOVA], see text for further details).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of psychophysical data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: Computed area under the curve was not significantly different for the five different stimuli (three single pruritogens and two combinations).
source: Peak magnitude of perceived sensation intensity (n = 29), (I) computed area under the curve (n = 17), or (J) duration of itch, stinging/pricking, or burn ratings (n = 17) were each not significantly different for the five different stimuli, that is, three single pruritogens and two combinations (repeated measures ANOVA [RMANOVA], see text for further details).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of psychophysical data shown in Figure 5I.

claim: Duration of itch, stinging/pricking, or burn ratings was not significantly different for the five different stimuli (three single pruritogens and two combinations).
source: Peak magnitude of perceived sensation intensity (n = 29), (I) computed area under the curve (n = 17), or (J) duration of itch, stinging/pricking, or burn ratings (n = 17) were each not significantly different for the five different stimuli, that is, three single pruritogens and two combinations (repeated measures ANOVA [RMANOVA], see text for further details).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of psychophysical data shown in Figure 5J.

claim: For peak ratings, 'sex' had a significant effect, with females giving significantly larger peak ratings than males.
source: Only for peak ratings, but not for AUC and duration,' sex' had a significant effect, with females giving significantly larger peak ratings than males (F(1,27)=6.53, p<0.017).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of psychophysical data.

claim: For peak ratings, the mean peak ratings for itch and pricking/stinging were each significantly greater than those for burning.
source: The mean peak ratings for itch and pricking/stinging were each significantly greater than those for burning (p<0.001, Bonferroni test)
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of psychophysical data.

claim: For peak ratings, mean peak ratings were significantly different only between ALA and BAM8-22.
source: For the factor 'stimulus,' mean peak ratings were significantly different only between ALA and BAM8-22 (p=0.01), and between ALA and the combined administration of all three pruritogens (p=0.03).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of psychophysical data.

claim: For peak ratings, mean peak ratings were significantly different between ALA and the combined administration of all three pruritogens.
source: For the factor 'stimulus,' mean peak ratings were significantly different only between ALA and BAM8-22 (p=0.01), and between ALA and the combined administration of all three pruritogens (p=0.03).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of psychophysical data.

claim: The mean AUC was significantly larger for itch than for burning.
source: The mean AUC was significantly larger for itch than for burning (p=0.012, Bonferroni test)
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of psychophysical data.

claim: Itch lasted significantly longer than burning.
source: and itch lasted significantly longer than burning (p<0.001, Bonferroni test).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of psychophysical data.

claim: No statistical differences were found between AUCs and durations of itch, pricking/stinging, and burning evoked by BAM8-22, ALA, HIS, and combinations thereof.
source: No statistical differences were found between AUCs and durations of itch, pricking/stinging, and burning evoked by BAM8-22, ALA, HIS, and combinations thereof (Figure 5I, J).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of psychophysical data shown in Figures 5I and 5J.

claim: A combination of pruritogens did not alter the magnitude or quality of sensations over those elicited by one of its component single pruritogens.
source: Thus, a combination of pruritogens did not alter the magnitude or quality of sensations over those elicited by one of its component single pruritogens.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the psychophysical data.

claim: Increasing the number of activated mechanosensitive nociceptive afferents by combining BAM8-22 and ALA and then adding in MIAs with HIS included in the mixture did not diminish itch and increase the magnitude of nociceptive sensations.
source: For example, increasing the number of activated mechanosensitive nociceptive afferents by combining BAM8-22 and ALA and then adding in MIAs with HIS included in the mixture did not diminish itch and increase the magnitude of nociceptive sensations.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the psychophysical data.

claim: Intradermal injection of combinations of pruritogens does not lead to an increased sensation of itch or to a diminished sensation of itch with an increase in nociceptive sensations.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that intradermal injection of combinations of pruritogens does not lead to an increased sensation of itch or, alternatively, to a diminished sensation of itch with an increase in nociceptive sensations.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the psychophysical data.

claim: There was a significant main effect of 'stimulus' for alloknesis.
source: There was a significant main effect of 'stimulus' for alloknesis (F(2.18,61.08) = 10.27, p<0.001)
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of psychophysical data on areas of dysesthesia.

claim: There was a significant main effect of 'stimulus' for hyperalgesia.
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of psychophysical data on areas of dysesthesia.

claim: There was a significant main effect of 'stimulus' for hyperknesis.
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of psychophysical data on areas of dysesthesia.

claim: There was a significant main effect of 'stimulus' for wheal.
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of psychophysical data on areas of wheal.

claim: There was a significant main effect of 'stimulus' for flare.
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of psychophysical data on areas of flare.

claim: The mean areas of alloknesis after HIS and the combined administration of the three pruritogens were significantly greater compared to those induced by BAM8-22, ALA, or BAM8-22+ALA.
source: The mean areas of alloknesis and hyperalgesia after HIS and the combined administration of the three pruritogens were significantly greater compared to those induced by BAM8-22, ALA, or BAM8-22+ALA (Figure 6A, see Supplementary file 2 for p-values).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of psychophysical data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The mean areas of hyperalgesia after HIS and the combined administration of the three pruritogens were significantly greater compared to those induced by BAM8-22, ALA, or BAM8-22+ALA.
source: The mean areas of alloknesis and hyperalgesia after HIS and the combined administration of the three pruritogens were significantly greater compared to those induced by BAM8-22, ALA, or BAM8-22+ALA (Figure 6A, see Supplementary file 2 for p-values).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of psychophysical data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: For hyperknesis, HIS and the triple combination of pruritogens each induced significantly larger areas than either ALA or BAM8-22 alone, but not compared to the combination of BAM8-22+ALA.
source: For hyperknesis, HIS and the triple combination of pruritogens each induced significantly larger areas than either ALA or BAM8-22 alone, but not compared to the combination of BAM8-22+ALA.
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of psychophysical data.

claim: The combination of BAM8-22+ALA did not demonstrate any significant increase in alloknesis, hyperalgesia, or hyperknesis compared to BAM8-22 or ALA administered alone.
source: Notably, the combination of BAM8-22+ALA did not demonstrate any significant increase in alloknesis, hyperalgesia, or hyperknesis compared to BAM8-22 or ALA administered alone.
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of psychophysical data.

claim: The combination of three pruritogens did not significantly enhance any of the dysesthesia areas compared to HIS alone.
source: The combination of three pruritogens also did not significantly enhance any of the dysesthesia areas compared to HIS alone.
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of psychophysical data.

claim: The mean areas of wheal and flare were significantly larger in response to HIS and to the combination of all three pruritogens than in response to either BAM8-22 or ALA alone, or their combination.
source: The mean areas of wheal and flare were significantly larger in response to HIS and to the combination of all three pruritogens than in response to either BAM8-22 or ALA alone, or their combination (Figure 6B; see Supplementary file 2 for p-values).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of psychophysical data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The combination of BAM8-22 + ALA did not significantly alter the areas of flare and wheal compared to each compound alone.
source: Furthermore, the combination of BAM8-22 + ALA did not significantly alter the areas of flare and wheal compared to each compound alone.
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of psychophysical data.

claim: The triple combination did not cause larger areas of wheal and flare than HIS alone.
source: Similarly, the triple combination did not cause larger areas of wheal and flare than HIS alone.
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of psychophysical data.

claim: The co-activation of different classes of CMHs or co-activation of CMHs and C-MIAs does not increase areas of dysesthesias, flare, and/or wheal in comparison to the activation of distinct classes of nociceptors alone.
source: We conclude that the co-activation of different classes of CMHs or co-activation of CMHs and C-MIAs does not increase areas of dysesthesias, flare, and/or wheal in comparison to the activation of distinct classes of nociceptors alone.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the psychophysical data on dysesthesias and skin reactions.

claim: MRGPRX1 and MRGPRD are predominantly co-expressed in human DRG.
source: Employing ISH, we found that MRGPRX1 and MRGPRD are predominantly co-expressed in human DRG, indicating that primate and mouse pruritogen receptors have different patterns of expression.
evidence: This is based on in situ hybridization data presented in the study.

claim: Primate and mouse pruritogen receptors have different patterns of expression.
source: Employing ISH, we found that MRGPRX1 and MRGPRD are predominantly co-expressed in human DRG, indicating that primate and mouse pruritogen receptors have different patterns of expression.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of expression patterns between primates and mice.

claim: The MRGPRX1 and MRGPRD agonists activated predominantly cutaneous polymodal C-fibers with some differences in BAM8-22 activating almost all and ALA stimulating a smaller defined subset of C-fibers.
source: Using electrophysiology, we discovered that the MRGPRX1 and MRGPRD agonists activated predominantly cutaneous polymodal C-fibers with some differences in BAM8-22 activating almost all and ALA stimulating a smaller defined subset of C-fibers.
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological recordings from nonhuman primates.

claim: Mixtures of pruritogens (ALA, BAM8-22, and HIS) elicit itch percepts similar to those evoked by singly applied pruritogens.
source: We observed that mixtures of these pruritogens elicit itch percepts similar to those evoked by singly applied pruritogens, suggesting that combined versus differential fiber activation does not have a large effect in shaping the quality of sensation.
evidence: This is based on psychophysical experiments with human subjects.

claim: Combined versus differential fiber activation does not have a large effect in shaping the quality of sensation.
source: We observed that mixtures of these pruritogens elicit itch percepts similar to those evoked by singly applied pruritogens, suggesting that combined versus differential fiber activation does not have a large effect in shaping the quality of sensation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the psychophysical data showing similar sensations for single and combined pruritogens.

claim: Primates lack the Mrgprc receptor or a differently named orthologous receptor.
source: However, primates lack the Mrgprc receptor or a differently named orthologous receptor and instead harbor a distinct subfamily of MRGPRs, named MRGPRX (Solinski et al., 2014), that is, clear orthologous receptors of this subfamily are absent in rodents (Zylka et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Solinski et al., 2014 and Zylka et al., 2003.

claim: Primates harbor a distinct subfamily of MRGPRs, named MRGPRX.
source: However, primates lack the Mrgprc receptor or a differently named orthologous receptor and instead harbor a distinct subfamily of MRGPRs, named MRGPRX (Solinski et al., 2014), that is, clear orthologous receptors of this subfamily are absent in rodents (Zylka et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Solinski et al., 2014 and Zylka et al., 2003.

claim: Clear orthologous receptors of the MRGPRX subfamily are absent in rodents.
source: However, primates lack the Mrgprc receptor or a differently named orthologous receptor and instead harbor a distinct subfamily of MRGPRs, named MRGPRX (Solinski et al., 2014), that is, clear orthologous receptors of this subfamily are absent in rodents (Zylka et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Solinski et al., 2014 and Zylka et al., 2003.

claim: MRGPRX1 in humans, like Mrgprc in mice, is activated by BAM8-22.
source: Despite this major difference in pruritogen receptor families between primates and rodents, a striking pharmacological similarity exists between receptors in primates and mice, with MRGPRX1 in humans, like Mrgprc in mice, being activated by BAM8-22 (Lembo et al., 2002) and MRGPRD being activated by ALA (Liu et al., 2012; Shinohara et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Lembo et al., 2002.

claim: MRGPRD is activated by ALA.
source: Despite this major difference in pruritogen receptor families between primates and rodents, a striking pharmacological similarity exists between receptors in primates and mice, with MRGPRX1 in humans, like Mrgprc in mice, being activated by BAM8-22 (Lembo et al., 2002) and MRGPRD being activated by ALA (Liu et al., 2012; Shinohara et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Liu et al., 2012 and Shinohara et al., 2004.

claim: MRGPRX1 is expressed in a subpopulation of human TRPV1-positive neurons.
source: Similar to the expression of Mrgprc in mice, we found that MRGPRX1 is expressed in a subpopulation of human TRPV1-positive neurons.
evidence: This is based on in situ hybridization data presented in the study.

claim: The MRGPRD expression largely overlaps with MRGPRX1 in human DRG.
source: However, we found that the MRGPRD expression largely overlaps with MRGPRX1 in human DRG.
evidence: This is based on in situ hybridization data presented in the study.

claim: The number of NPPB+ human DRG neurons (9.8%) corresponds well with the number of Nppb+ neurons found in mouse DRG neurons.
source: However, in a previous study (Solinski et al., 2019a), we found that the number of NPPB+ human DRG neurons (9.8%) corresponds well with the number of Nppb+ neurons found in mouse DRG neurons.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Solinski et al., 2019a.

claim: About four out of five NPPB+ human DRG neurons co-express MRGPRX1.
source: As about four out of five NPPB+ human DRG neurons co-express MRGPRX1, the MRGPRX1/MRGPRD+ population is about 8% of all DRG neurons.
evidence: This is based on in situ hybridization data presented in the study.

claim: The MRGPRX1/MRGPRD+ population is about 8% of all DRG neurons.
source: As about four out of five NPPB+ human DRG neurons co-express MRGPRX1, the MRGPRX1/MRGPRD+ population is about 8% of all DRG neurons.
evidence: This is an inference based on the proportion of NPPB+ neurons and their co-expression with MRGPRX1.

claim: The overlapping expression of MRGPRD and MRGPRX1 was observed in macaque DRG neurons, indicating a conserved expression pattern in the primate lineage.
source: Of note, we also observed the overlapping expression of MRGPRD and MRGPRX1 in macaque DRG neurons, indicating a conserved expression pattern in the primate lineage.
evidence: This is based on in situ hybridization data from macaque DRG.

claim: The expression pattern of MRGPRD and MRGPRX1 in primates is dramatically different from that found in mice, where Mrgprd is present in a distinct subclass of neurons that do not express Mrgprc and do not express Trpv1.
source: However, this expression pattern is dramatically different from that found in mice, where Mrgprd is present in a distinct subclass of neurons that do not express Mrgprc and do not express Trpv1 (Zylka et al., 2003).
evidence: This is a comparison of expression patterns between primates and mice supported by a citation to Zylka et al., 2003.

claim: MRGPRX1-positive human DRG neurons express NPPB.
source: Previously, we reported that MRGPRX1-positive human DRG neurons express NPPB and that these cells express additional pruritogen receptors, HRH1 and IL31RA (Solinski et al., 2019a).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Solinski et al., 2019a.

claim: MRGPRX1-positive human DRG neurons express additional pruritogen receptors, HRH1 and IL31RA.
source: Previously, we reported that MRGPRX1-positive human DRG neurons express NPPB and that these cells express additional pruritogen receptors, HRH1 and IL31RA (Solinski et al., 2019a).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Solinski et al., 2019a.

claim: In mice, Nppb and Il31ra are expressed in a class of neurons distinct from those that express either Mrgprc or Mrgprd.
source: Again, this expression pattern is different from that found in mice where Nppb and Il31ra are expressed in a class of neurons distinct from those that express either Mrgprc or Mrgprd (Dong et al., 2001; Nguyen et al., 2017; Usoskin et al., 2015; Zylka et al., 2003; Zylka et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies in mice.

claim: Nppb was shown to be necessary for the transmission of pruritic signals between primary afferents and second order spinal cord neurons in mice.
source: Interestingly, Nppb was shown to be necessary for the transmission of pruritic signals between primary afferents and second order spinal cord neurons in mice (Mishra and Hoon, 2013)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Mishra and Hoon, 2013.

claim: The MRGPRX1/MRGPRD/NPPB neuronal population is involved in primate itch.
source: which in turn is suggestive of the idea that the MRGPRX1/MRGPRD/NPPB neuronal population is also involved in primate itch.
evidence: This is an inference based on the expression pattern and the role of Nppb in mice.

claim: At least at the level of the DRG soma, pruritogen receptors are expressed in a largely overlapping fashion in humans.
source: Thus, our findings expand our previous knowledge on human sensory neurons and indicate that, at least at the level of the DRG soma, pruritogen receptors are expressed in a largely overlapping fashion in humans.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the in situ hybridization data.

claim: ALA or BAM8-22 did not activate A-fiber nociceptors.
source: Interestingly, ALA or BAM8-22 did not activate A-fiber nociceptors, and C-MIAs were activated rarely by BAM8-22 (2/6 responsive), and not at all by ALA.
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological recordings from A-fiber nociceptors.

claim: C-MIAs were activated rarely by BAM8-22 (2/6 responsive).
source: Interestingly, ALA or BAM8-22 did not activate A-fiber nociceptors, and C-MIAs were activated rarely by BAM8-22 (2/6 responsive), and not at all by ALA.
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological recordings from C-MIAs.

claim: BAM8-22 could elicit a small flare (~5 cm2 on average) in psychophysical experiments.
source: Because BAM8-22 could elicit a small flare (~5 cm2 on average) in our psychophysical experiments, we cannot rule out the possibility of an indirect C-MIA activation via mast cells (Solinski et al., 2013; Subramanian et al., 2011).
evidence: This is based on psychophysical data from the study.

claim: CMHs are excited by intradermal injections of ALA and BAM8-22.
source: In contrast, we show that CMHs are excited by intradermal injections of ALA and BAM8-22.
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological recordings from CMHs.

claim: About 60% of cutaneous CMHs (nearly all QCs but only 23% of SCs) are sensitive to ALA in monkeys.
source: Confirming our earlier results (Wooten et al., 2014), we found that the MRGPRD agonist ALA preferentially activated QCs, indicating that about 60% of cutaneous CMHs (nearly all QCs but only 23% of SCs) are sensitive to ALA in monkeys.
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological recordings and confirmed by a citation to Wooten et al., 2014.

claim: BAM8-22 activated a large proportion of QCs (72% of QCs responded to BAM8-22).
source: In agreement with our human expression data, BAM8-22 also activated a large proportion of QCs (72% of QCs responded to BAM8-22), indicating that MRGPRD and MRGPRX1 are co-expressed in this functional class of cutaneous primary afferents.
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological recordings from QCs.

claim: MRGPRD and MRGPRX1 are co-expressed in QCs.
source: In agreement with our human expression data, BAM8-22 also activated a large proportion of QCs (72% of QCs responded to BAM8-22), indicating that MRGPRD and MRGPRX1 are co-expressed in this functional class of cutaneous primary afferents.
evidence: This is an inference based on the electrophysiological responses of QCs to both ALA and BAM8-22.

claim: BAM8-22 evoked action potentials in the SC class of CMHs (93% of SCs responded to BAM8-22) that was largely unresponsive to ALA.
source: Surprisingly, given our expression data, we observed that BAM8-22 evoked APs in the SC class of CMHs (93% of SCs responded to BAM8-22) that was largely unresponsive to ALA.
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological recordings from SCs.

claim: BAM8-22-induced responses in SCs were about twice as large as in QCs.
source: Furthermore, BAM8-22-induced responses in SCs were about twice as large as in QCs.
evidence: This is based on comparison of electrophysiological responses between SCs and QCs.
